# 1 Types of Relative Clauses

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What a relative clause does

A **relative clause** is a clause that gives more information about a noun. It begins with *who*, *which*, *that*, *where*, *whose*, and so on. Those opening words are how you spot one: the clause attaches itself to a noun already in the sentence and tells you something further about it.

The guide divides relative clauses into two kinds, and the division is not about what the clause says but about how tightly the sentence needs it.

## Non-essential (nonrestrictive) clauses

A **non-essential clause**, also called a **nonrestrictive clause**, is a clause that gives more information, and it also uses a comma. The guide's example:

> 'My brother, who lives in California, is visiting us next week'

The pair of commas fences the clause off from the rest of the sentence. Lift *who lives in California* out and the sentence still says who is visiting: the brother is already identified by *my brother*, so the clause is an addition rather than a requirement.

## Essential (restrictive) clauses

An **essential clause**, also called a **restrictive clause**, is a clause that does not give extra information, and it takes no comma. The guide's example:

> The car that is parked outside belongs to my neighbour.

Here *that is parked outside* is not decoration. It is what tells you which car is meant, so it cannot be lifted out and it is not sealed off with commas.

## Telling the two apart

The visible difference is the punctuation, and the punctuation follows from the job the clause is doing. When the guide says a non-essential clause "gives more information" and an essential clause "doesn't give extra information", *extra* is the operative word: extra means removable. Information the sentence cannot do without is not extra, and a clause carrying it is written without commas.

So the test in an exam is to read the sentence with the clause taken out. If the sentence still points at the same person or thing, the clause is non-essential and needs its commas. If the sentence goes vague about which one you mean, the clause is essential and the commas must go.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Relative clause** | A clause that gives more information about a noun; begins with *who*, *which*, *that*, *where*, *whose*, etc. |
| **Non-essential clause (nonrestrictive clause)** | A clause that gives more information; also uses a comma |
| **Essential clause (restrictive clause)** | A clause that doesn't give extra information; no comma |

# 2 Parallel Structure

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The definition

**Parallel structure** means using the same grammatical form for similar elements in a sentence. Elements count as similar when the sentence treats them as equals — the items of a list, the parts of a series — and the rule asks that equal elements be dressed in equal grammar.

## Fixing parallel structure

The repair the guide gives is a single instruction: ensure each list or series uses the same form. You find the series, look at the form of the first item, and put every later item into that same form.

The guide's example:

> 'She likes reading, writing, and running.'

Three items sit in the series and all three are *-ing* forms. Nothing in the sentence is doing anything cleverer than that, which is the point — parallelism is not an ornament but the plainest way of showing a reader that three things are being offered on the same footing. Break the pattern for one item and the reader's eye catches on it, because the grammar has stopped saying what the sentence means.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Parallel structure** | Using the same grammatical form for similar elements in a sentence |

# 3 Journalistic and Narrative Voice

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide flags this section with a note worth keeping: it is not sure the material will be tested, but you still need to know it.

## The two voices side by side

The difference between the two voices starts with what each is for, and everything else — stance, sentence length, structure, what the writing leans on for evidence — follows from that purpose.

| Aspect | Journalistic voice | Narrative voice |
|---|---|---|
| Aim | Inform the audience about facts, events, issues | Tell a story |
| Stance | Generally objective and neutral | Subjective, reflective, allowing emotional depth |
| Focus | Facts, events, issues | The character's thoughts, feelings, motivations |
| Structure | Follows the inverted pyramid structure | Follows a narrative arc |
| Sentences | Concise and straightforward; sentences are often short | More varied and flexible; sentences can be longer and more complex, often employing literary devices |
| What it relies on | Quotes and statistics, heavily | Rich, evocative description |

## Journalistic voice

Journalism sets out to inform an audience about facts, events and issues, and its habits are the habits of a writer who wants to be believed rather than admired. The voice is generally objective and neutral. The prose is concise and straightforward, and sentences are often short.

Its structure is the **inverted pyramid**: the important information comes first. A reader who stops after one paragraph should already have the substance of the story, so the writer front-loads rather than building to a conclusion.

It relies heavily on quotes and statistics. That reliance is how the neutral stance is maintained in practice — the writing puts named sources and figures in front of the reader instead of the writer's own impressions.

## Narrative voice

Narrative writing aims to tell a story, and it follows a narrative arc rather than the inverted pyramid — which means it is built the opposite way round, holding material back so the shape of the story can do its work.

The voice is subjective and reflective, and that is what allows emotional depth. It focuses on a character's thoughts, feelings and motivations, the things a neutral report leaves out. Its style is more varied and flexible: sentences can be longer and more complex, and often employ literary devices. It uses rich, evocative description to create atmosphere and evoke emotion.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Journalistic voice** | A voice that informs the audience about facts, events and issues; generally objective and neutral, concise and straightforward, following the inverted pyramid and relying heavily on quotes and statistics |
| **Narrative voice** | A voice that aims to tell a story; subjective and reflective, following a narrative arc, focusing on a character's thoughts, feelings and motivations, and using rich, evocative description |
| **Inverted pyramid structure** | A structure in which the important information comes first |

# 4 The Book of Unknown Americans: Context and Plot

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The novel at a glance

| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| When written | 2009–2013 |
| When published | 2014 |
| Genre | Literary fiction |
| Setting | Newark, Delaware, U.S.A. |
| Climax | Believing his daughter Maribel is in danger, Arturo sets out to confront the boy he believes is responsible and he is shot and killed along the way |
| Antagonist | Garrett Miller |

The gap between when the novel was written and when it was set matters less here than the setting itself. Newark, Delaware is not a border town or a great immigrant city; it is an ordinary American place, and the novel puts its immigrant families there rather than anywhere symbolic.

## Plot summary

The novel follows Arturo and Alma Rivera, who move from Mexico to Newark, Delaware with their teenage daughter Maribel in hopes of healing her after a traumatic brain injury. That hope is the engine of everything that follows: the family has not come for work in the ordinary sense but for a school.

Maribel attends a special school while her parents struggle to adapt. Arturo works long hours at a mushroom farm, and Alma faces deep homesickness. Their lives intertwine with their neighbours Celia and Rafael Toro, and their son Mayor, who becomes close to Maribel despite her condition.

As Mayor and Maribel grow closer, they are targeted by a school bully, Garrett Miller, who eventually assaults Maribel. Alma tries to shield her daughter, but the incident and other tensions escalate. Arturo loses his job, and the family's American dream begins to unravel — the school that brought them to Delaware depends on the work that has just gone.

Meanwhile, Mayor defies his parents, steals a car, and takes Maribel out to experience her first snowfall, causing panic when she doesn't return home. Arturo, trying to find Maribel, confronts Garrett's family and is fatally shot by Garrett's father. The two strands of the plot close on each other here: the boy's romantic gesture and the father's fear of the bully meet in the same night.

The tragedy devastates the community, and Alma and Maribel prepare to return to Mexico. The neighbours raise money to help them bring Arturo's body back home — the community that could not protect the family is nevertheless what makes the journey home possible.

## The ending

As Alma and Maribel leave, Alma realises that Maribel, despite her injury, has always been herself, and they drive on, carrying their loss and hope into the future. The realisation is the resolution of Alma's own story rather than of the plot: the family came north to make Maribel into who she had been, and Alma leaves understanding that she had not been lost in the first place.

| **Setting** | Newark, Delaware, U.S.A. |

| **Antagonist** | Garrett Miller |

# 5 Characters in The Book of Unknown Americans

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Each of the guide's eight major characters is set out the same way: the role they play in the novel, the themes they carry, the arc they travel, and what they symbolise. Read the four together — the symbolism is usually the arc restated at the level of the whole immigrant experience.

## 1. Alma Rivera — The Protective and Guilt-Ridden Mother

**Role:** protagonist, matriarch of the Rivera family. **Themes:** isolation vs. community, maternal love, guilt, fear, adaptation.

Alma begins the story consumed by guilt over her daughter's accident, which propels her to seek a better life in the U.S. Though she finds community at the Redwood Apartments and builds deep friendships, especially with Celia, Alma remains emotionally isolated. Her overprotectiveness and silence about Garrett's assault on Maribel — rooted in shame and fear — ultimately leads to tragic consequences. The silence is the hinge of her arc: the same guilt that brought the family north is what stops her speaking when speaking would have helped. Yet Alma also learns to reframe her understanding of Maribel, accepting her daughter not as "lost" but transformed.

Alma symbolises the sacrifices and quiet resilience of immigrant mothers, as well as the inner conflict between personal guilt and societal survival.

## 2. Arturo Rivera — The Selfless Father and Martyr

**Role:** breadwinner of the Rivera family. **Themes:** sacrifice, family, the American Dream, dignity.

Arturo is hardworking and selfless, labouring in grim conditions to provide for Maribel's education. His enduring optimism and humour provide emotional warmth to the family. However, his tragic death following a misunderstanding with Garrett's family positions him as a martyr — a man who dies trying to protect what little hope he had built.

Arturo represents both the dream and the futility of the American immigrant experience: the idea that hard work doesn't always yield justice or security in a broken system. He is the character on whom the novel's central promise is tested, and the test fails.

## 3. Maribel Rivera — The Symbol of Lost and Reclaimed Identity

**Role:** catalyst of the plot, daughter of Alma and Arturo. **Themes:** disability, trauma, identity, love, coming of age.

Once vibrant and rebellious, Maribel becomes quiet and confused after her injury. While many treat her as incapable, her relationship with Mayor reveals her inner self and potential for healing — Mayor is the one character who addresses her as a person rather than a condition. By the end, she reclaims aspects of her identity, and Alma realises she never truly lost her.

Maribel embodies both the fragility and resilience of personhood. She challenges societal definitions of value and capability.

## 4. Mayor Toro — The Sensitive Adolescent in Search of Purpose

**Role:** Alma's narrator counterpart, and Maribel's friend and love interest. **Themes:** adolescence, masculinity, love, rebellion, perception.

Mayor begins as a boy trapped by his father's unrealistic expectations and his own self-doubt. His love for Maribel becomes a vehicle for asserting his identity, but also exposes his immaturity and naivety. His idealised love leads to tension and tragedy, but also growth.

Mayor represents the second-generation immigrant youth, caught between two cultures and expectations, struggling to find his own path. Note that he is Alma's narrator counterpart: the novel's two central voices are a mother of the first generation and a son of the second.

## 5. Celia Toro — The Bridge Between Cultures

**Role:** Mayor's mother, Alma's best friend. **Themes:** friendship, gender roles, nostalgia, endurance.

Celia is nurturing and pragmatic, supporting her family and friends with wisdom and kindness. She balances emotional intelligence with practicality, especially in her friendship with Alma and in handling her husband Rafael's temperament. She also symbolises the longing for home — one that no longer exists, which is what makes the nostalgia permanent rather than curable.

Celia is the emotional bedrock of the community and an anchor to the immigrant experience of lost roots and found kinship.

## 6. Rafael "Rafa" Toro — The Disillusioned Patriarch

**Role:** Mayor's father. **Themes:** masculinity, authority, trauma, generational conflict.

Rafa's harshness comes from a desire to see his family thrive, shaped by his traumatic past. His rigidity and obsession with success create conflict, especially with Mayor. He embodies the difficulty many first-generation immigrants face when reconciling past hardship with a new culture.

Rafa symbolises both the trauma of war and migration, and the dangers of unyielding patriarchal expectations. His demands on Mayor are the same demands the migration made on him, passed down a generation.

## 7. Garrett Miller — The Embodiment of Threat and Privilege

**Role:** local bully and antagonist. **Themes:** racism, privilege, danger, repression.

Garrett is mostly static — he represents the looming threat to immigrant safety rather than a character who changes. His harassment of Maribel and subsequent confrontation with Arturo result in tragedy. Yet glimpses of his own troubled family life suggest a cycle of abuse and neglect.

Garrett personifies unchecked privilege, toxic masculinity, and the dangers of silence and complicity. The silence in that list is not only his: it is also Alma's, which is why he functions as the novel's antagonist rather than merely its villain.

## 8. Quisqueya Solis — The Masked Survivor

**Role:** gossip, and narrator of her own story. **Themes:** shame, survival, identity.

Outwardly flamboyant and dramatic, Quisqueya hides a history of abuse and trauma. Her need for control and social status masks a painful past. That she narrates her own story is part of the point: the community sees the gossip, and only her own chapter shows what the manner is covering.

She represents the complexities of identity formation and the need to rewrite one's narrative to survive.

## Supporting characters as community voices

Each minor character at Redwood Apartments adds texture to the immigrant mosaic.

| Character | What they contribute |
|---|---|
| Benny Quinto | A former seminarian turned smuggler and prayer leader; symbolises contradiction and redemption |
| Gustavo Milhojas | A janitor with a tragic past and enduring hope; reflects perseverance and generational sacrifice |
| Adolfo "Fito" Angelino | The kind landlord; symbolises the evolution of the American Dream |
| Nelia Zafón and José Mercado | Artists thwarted by systems of oppression; embody the theme of unrealised potential |
| Micho Alvarez | A photographer and activist; voices political resistance and cultural pride |

## Keywords

| **Alma Rivera** | The Protective and Guilt-Ridden Mother; protagonist and matriarch of the Rivera family |
| **Arturo Rivera** | The Selfless Father and Martyr; breadwinner of the Rivera family |
| **Maribel Rivera** | The Symbol of Lost and Reclaimed Identity; catalyst of the plot, daughter of Alma and Arturo |
| **Mayor Toro** | The Sensitive Adolescent in Search of Purpose; Alma's narrator counterpart and Maribel's friend/love interest |

# 6 Key Themes

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide gives six themes, and for each one it names the characters and situations the theme is explored through. Those names are the useful part: a theme statement on its own earns nothing in an answer, and the evidence the guide attaches is what turns it into a paragraph.

## 1. Immigration and the American Dream

**Explored through:** nearly every character, particularly Alma and Arturo Rivera.

Many characters came to the U.S. seeking opportunity, safety, or a better future for their children. Yet the reality they face — poor working conditions, poverty, and social alienation — shows the complexity and sometimes the futility of the "American Dream." The theme is therefore not the dream itself but the distance between what was promised and what arrives.

Arturo's tragic death underscores how even hardworking, optimistic immigrants can be thwarted by systemic barriers and prejudice. He is the guide's proof of the point, because nothing in his conduct explains what happens to him.

## 2. Isolation vs. Community

**Explored through:** Alma Rivera, Celia Toro, the Redwood Apartments residents.

The immigrants are isolated by language, culture, and trauma. Alma feels especially alone due to guilt and fear — her isolation is doubled, since it comes from inside her as well as from the country she has moved to.

However, the Redwood Apartments become a small, vibrant community where immigrants support one another in ways that are emotionally and materially vital. Both halves of the theme are true at once, which is why the guide states it as a versus rather than as a progression from one to the other.

## 3. Love and Relationships

**Explored through:** Mayor and Maribel's budding romance; Alma and Arturo's marriage; the Toro family dynamics.

Love is shown in its many forms: romantic, parental, platonic. The novel questions what it means to love someone who is changed by trauma, as Alma does with Maribel.

Mayor's love for Maribel becomes both redemptive and problematic, raising ethical questions about consent, care, and agency. That double judgement is the theme's substance — the same relationship that shows Maribel as a person also puts her in danger.

## 4. Trauma and Recovery

**Explored through:** Maribel's brain injury; Quisqueya's childhood abuse; immigrants' stories of war, loss, and displacement.

The characters carry emotional and physical scars. Maribel's recovery is slow and nonlinear, and each immigrant's trauma affects how they integrate into American society — the past is not something the migration leaves behind.

The novel suggests that healing is possible, but it requires patience, understanding, and community. Read against theme 2, that makes the Redwood Apartments a condition of recovery rather than merely a comfort.

## 5. Family and Sacrifice

**Explored through:** Alma and Arturo's sacrifices for Maribel; Rafa's demands of his sons; Celia's longing for her family.

Immigrant parents often sacrifice everything to give their children better lives, even at great personal cost. Alma's guilt and resolve to help Maribel drive the family's migration, and Arturo ultimately pays with his life. The cost in this novel is not metaphorical, which is what separates this theme from the American Dream theme it sits beside.

## 6. Identity and Belonging

**Explored through:** Mayor's adolescent insecurities; Rafa's rejection of his "gringo" label; Celia's nostalgia for Panamá.

The guide's three examples are one from each generation and each direction of feeling: a son unsure of who he is, a father refusing the identity the new country offers him, and a mother longing for the country she left.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Immigration and the American Dream** | Explored through nearly every character, particularly Alma and Arturo Rivera: the gap between the opportunity sought and the poor working conditions, poverty and social alienation found |
| **Isolation vs. Community** | Explored through Alma Rivera, Celia Toro and the Redwood Apartments residents: immigrants isolated by language, culture and trauma, yet supporting one another in vital ways |
| **Love and Relationships** | Explored through Mayor and Maribel's romance, Alma and Arturo's marriage and the Toro family dynamics: love in its romantic, parental and platonic forms |
| **Trauma and Recovery** | Explored through Maribel's brain injury, Quisqueya's childhood abuse and immigrants' stories of war, loss and displacement: healing is possible but requires patience, understanding and community |
| **Family and Sacrifice** | Explored through Alma and Arturo's sacrifices for Maribel, Rafa's demands of his sons and Celia's longing for her family: parents sacrifice everything for their children at great personal cost |
| **Identity and Belonging** | Explored through Mayor's adolescent insecurities, Rafa's rejection of his "gringo" label and Celia's nostalgia for Panamá |

# 7 Lexis

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide's lexis list is the critical vocabulary — the terms you use to *write about* the novel, as distinct from the words you meet inside it. Each term comes with a model sentence showing the term in use, and those sentences are worth studying as much as the definitions: they show the register these words belong to.

## Voice

**Voice** is the distinct personality or style of an author as expressed in their writing. The guide's sentence:

> The author's voice in the novel captures the struggles of adolescence with humor and poignancy.

Voice is a property of the writing rather than of the events, which is why the sentence credits it with capturing something the plot merely contains. The journalistic and narrative voices set out earlier in this guide are two settings this quality can take.

## Auto theory

**Auto theory** is a concept that emphasises self reflection and personal experience in understanding art and literature. The guide's sentence:

> In her essay, she applied auto theory to explore how her own upbringing influenced her interpretation of the text.

The term names a method of criticism: the reader's own life is treated as evidence about the text rather than as an intrusion on it.

## Assimilation

**Assimilation** is the process by which individuals or groups adopt the cultural norms of another group, often losing their original identity. The guide's sentence:

> The story explores the challenges of assimilation faced by immigrant families in a new country.

Note the *often losing their original identity* in the definition. Assimilation as this guide defines it is not simply arrival or adjustment; it carries a cost, which is what makes it a term of analysis and not a neutral description.

## Cultural monolith

**Cultural monolith** is the idea that a culture is uniform and unchanging, ignoring its diversity and complexity. The guide's sentence:

> The film critiques the concept of a cultural monolith by showcasing the varied experiences within a single community.

The sentence also shows how the term is normally used: writers invoke a cultural monolith in order to argue against it, by producing the internal variety the idea denies.

## Passing (for white)

**Passing (for white)** is the act of a person of non-white ethnicity being perceived as white, often to gain social advantages. The guide's sentence:

> The protagonist grapples with the implications of passing for white in a society that values whiteness.

The definition ties the act to advantage, and the sentence ties the advantage to a society that values whiteness — the practice is a response to a hierarchy rather than a preference.

## Point of view

**Point of view** is the perspective from which a story is told, influencing how events and characters are perceived. The guide's sentence:

> The shift in point of view in the novel allows readers to understand the motivations of both the hero and the antagonist.

The word *influencing* is the examinable part. Point of view is not just who is speaking but what that choice does to the reader's judgement, and a shift in it changes who the reader is able to sympathise with.

## Double consciousness

**Double consciousness** is a concept describing the internal conflict experienced by marginalised groups in a dominant culture, particularly in understanding one's identity. The guide's sentence:

> The character's sense of double consciousness highlights the struggle between their cultural heritage and societal expectations.

The conflict is internal, which is the distinguishing feature: it is not a clash between a character and other people but a division inside a single person, who sees themselves both from within their heritage and through the dominant culture's eyes.

## Latino

**Latino** is a term used to describe people of Latin American origin or descent, encompassing a diverse range of cultures and identities. The guide's sentence:

> The anthology features stories from various Latino authors, each offering unique perspectives on identity and belonging.

The *diverse range* in the definition is deliberate and reads against the cultural monolith defined above: the term covers many cultures and identities rather than naming one.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Voice** | The distinct personality or style of an author as expressed in their writing |
| **Auto theory** | A concept that emphasises self reflection and personal experience in understanding art and literature |
| **Assimilation** | The process by which individuals or groups adopt the cultural norms of another group, often losing their original identity |
| **Cultural monolith** | The idea that a culture is uniform and unchanging, ignoring its diversity and complexity |
| **Passing (for white)** | The act of a person of non-white ethnicity being perceived as white, often to gain social advantages |
| **Point of view** | The perspective from which a story is told, influencing how events and characters are perceived |
| **Double consciousness** | A concept describing the internal conflict experienced by marginalised groups in a dominant culture, particularly in understanding one's identity |
| **Latino** | A term used to describe people of Latin American origin or descent, encompassing a diverse range of cultures and identities |

# 8 Vocabulary in Context

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Every word on the guide's vocabulary list arrives inside a sentence from the novel rather than on its own. Learn them that way. The sentence tells you the company the word keeps — what kind of subject it takes, whether it describes a feeling or an action — and a definition memorised without it is easy to recognise and hard to use. The words are given below in the guide's own order, each with the guide's definition and the guide's sentence.

## Feeling and reaction

**Surge** — a sudden and powerful increase or rise.

> I lay there listening to the soft chorus of Maribel's and Arturo's long, even breaths. In and out. The surge of possibility. The tug of doubt. Had we done the right thing, coming here?

**Ambivalent** — experiencing mixed feelings; often feelings of both liking and disliking.

> When he looked ambivalent, I lied and said, "I've been practicing with my dad at home. Even he thinks I'm getting better."

**Bewildered** — confused.

> It was a story about how Yu Li came to the United States from China with his parents. He went to school one day and some of the kids taunted him and some of them were kind. But Yu Li didn't know English, so he was bewildered.

**Meagerness** — a small amount; not enough.

> But when Arturo didn't say anything, I felt acutely the meagerness of it, the insufficiency. We wanted more. We wanted what we had come here for.

**Compliant** — willing to follow rules, standards, or requests.

> She resisted, she was confused, and then, suddenly, something would snap back into place and she was compliant, agreeable.

## Pleading, anger and repair

**Imploring** — begging or pleading earnestly and desperately.

> And sometimes I went to the small church we had found, St. Thomas More Oratory, with its water-stained drop ceiling and its folding chairs in place of pews, and sat alone in the empty sanctuary, reciting the same prayers over and over, imploring God to listen.

**Indignation** — strong displeasure or anger aroused by something seen as unfair.

> The boy said something in English, something unintelligible to me, but I could hear the indignation in his tone, and without thinking, I turned and spat in his face.

**Conception** — the process of conceiving or forming an idea; the beginning or origin of something.

> Arturo usually frowned when she did those things—they didn't fit the Mexican conception of what girls could and should do—but I loved that about Maribel.

**Reproach** — expressing disapproval.

> "I'm sorry," I murmured, the combined weight of horror and reproach pressing against my chest.

**Rehabilitation** — the process of restoring someone to health.

> After weeks of rehabilitation, after working with a psychologist and a speech language pathologist and the doctor, all they could tell us was things like: She struggles with finding the right words sometimes, and that will likely persist.

## Force, appetite and bravado

**Machismo** — a strong or exaggerated sense of masculinity, often characterized by dominance.

> In the time that he and my mom had been gone, I'd talked myself into the idea that maybe my dad would be proud of me—just a little bit—when he found out I'd gotten into a fight. Maybe it proved I had a little bit of machismo in me after all.

This is the one word on the list that names a theme the guide sets out elsewhere: masculinity is listed among the themes carried by both Mayor and Rafa.

**Indestructible** — impossible to destroy or damage.

> We believed we were special. We believed we were indestructible. But after the accident, under the gathering clouds of fate, something changed.

**Careened** — to swerve or lurch while moving at speed; out of control. The guide prints the definition as "to fall into someone or something"; that is an error — careen means to swerve or lurch, which is what the car in the sentence below does as it passes.

> He careened around us and, as he passed by, yelled out his open window, "Learn how to f**king drive!"

**Lusted** — a strong desire for someone or something.

> I had a feeling she'd been one of the popular girls, the one all the guys lusted over.

**Revelry** — noisy festivities; playful.

> And then, in the middle of the revelry, we heard a knock at the door.

## Blame, judgement and speaking out

**Legitimate** — real or true.

> A guard examined the driver's papers, which were legitimate. The guard did not know we were in the back of the van.

**Exonerated** — to clear of blame.

> My dad glanced at my mom and for one delirious second I thought I was off the hook, that somehow I'd exonerated myself, and that we could all just go back to business as usual.

**Virtuous** — full of integrity; showing high moral standards.

> He believed a man should work hard with his hands, that toil and sweat were evidence of a virtuous life.

**Advocating** — publicly recommend or support.

> Now I work with a group in Wilmington that's advocating for legislation reform for immigrants.

**Misguided** — showing bad judgement or reasoning.

> What did it matter, my instinct to protect him, my misguided idea that somehow by keeping all of this from him, I could prove that I was capable, I could prove that I could take care of our daughter even though I had failed her so terribly before?

## Sympathy, impulse and harm

**Condolence** — an expression or sympathy, especially during a time of death.

> She apologized over and over, and though at first I mistook her apologies for condolences, I realized soon enough that she believed she had a role in what had happened—or maybe that Mayor did

**Impetuous** — done quickly without thought.

> Not exactly the girl she used to be before the accident, which was the girl I thought I had been searching for, but my Maribel, brave and impetuous and kind.

**Assaulted** — physically attacked.

> We don't deal with teenage relationships here. Unless he assaulted her in some way, or unless he made some kind of verbal threat, there's nothing we can do.

**Erupt** — to burst forth suddenly and violently.

> My hip throbbed. Coach blew his whistle and jogged in to untangle us. The girls erupted in laughter.

**Discarded** — to get rid of or throw away.

> Later, when he stopped again and pointed to a discarded kitchen table, and later again at a mattress propped up like a sliding board against someone's mailbox, we understood what to do and loaded them into the truck.

## Cold, pain and comfort

**Barren** — empty or lacking in vegetation, often land that is unable to support plant life.

> It was snowing when we arrived—Enrique kept complaining that the snow was going to mess up his beloved Adidas sneakers—and everything was so colorless and barren that it looked like the moon.

**Constrict** — to tighten, squeeze, or flatten.

> He walked closer, and I felt the world constrict, my heart pulsing against my ribs. When we were only an arm's length apart, he stopped.

**Excruciating** — extremely intense or painful.

> It was a lovely thought, but hearing Arturo's optimism bubble to the surface, hearing the rawness of it, was excruciating.

**Console** — to comfort.

> At the hospital, Officer Mora, the same officer I had spoken with at the station months earlier, tried to console me.

**Indisputable** — not able to dispute or argue against.

> "She's getting better," I said, as if by repeating it enough, I could somehow make it part of the public record, an indisputable fact.

# 1 Lexis Terms: The Vocabulary of Comics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Why the guide begins with vocabulary

The review guide opens with lexis rather than with plot, and the ordering is worth taking seriously. *City of Glass* is a graphic novel, so a large share of the evidence available in the exam is drawn rather than written. An answer that says the pictures grow strange as Quinn falls apart has noticed something true but has no vocabulary to pin it to; the same observation made in terms of **panels**, **gutters** and **tiers** can be argued and marked. The eight terms below are the guide's working vocabulary for describing what is physically on the page.

## The terms

**Border** — the line or frame around a comic panel. The border is the edge of what the reader is permitted to see, so it is also a device for enclosing a character: a figure shut inside a tight frame reads differently from the same figure in an open one.

**Gutter** — the space between comic panels where the reader infers movement or time passing. *Infers* is the load-bearing word in the guide's definition. Nothing is drawn in a gutter, so whatever happens between one panel and the next is supplied by the reader, not by the artist. This is why the guide can later claim that the graphic-novel form itself emphasises constructed realities: the form obliges the reader to build part of the story, which is a pointed thing to ask of a reader in a book about whether reality can be trusted.

**Speech Bubble** — a rounded shape that contains a character's spoken words. Because the bubble is drawn, speech in a comic has a *shape* as well as a content, and the shape can be altered. That is the mechanism behind Peter Stillman Jr.'s dialogue, whose strangeness is visible in the bubbles themselves before the reader has parsed a word of it.

**Emanata** — visual symbols (e.g., sweat drops, motion lines) showing emotion or movement. Emanata are the comic's way of externalising an internal state without narrating it.

**Tier** — a horizontal row of comic panels. The tier is the unit of rhythm on a page: a page of regular tiers reads steadily, and a page whose tiers break down reads as disorder.

**Icon** — a simplified image that represents a character, object, or idea. An icon is not a picture of a thing so much as a stand-in for it, which is what allows a fingerprint, an egg or a maze to carry an argument in this book rather than merely decorate a panel.

**Sound Effect** — onomatopoeic words (e.g., BOOM, splash) that convey sound within the scene. Note that the sound effect is a *word* doing the work of a *noise* — text asked to be something other than text, in a novel preoccupied with what words can and cannot do.

**Caption** — text (often in a box) that provides narration or context outside of dialogue. The caption is the guide's dividing line between a character speaking and a narrator narrating: dialogue goes in bubbles, narration goes in captions. Keep the two apart when writing about a page, because a shift from one to the other is a shift in who is telling the story.

## The artist and the style

The guide names two adaptors with distinct jobs — **Paul Karasik** as Writer/Adapter and **David Mazzucchelli** as Artist — and the practice set tests whether that division is understood.

> **6.** The distinctive visual style of the graphic novel, characterized by stark shadows, clean lines, and deliberate pacing, is primarily the work of: a) Paul Auster b) Paul Karasik c) David Mazzucchelli d) Art Spiegelman

The answer is **c) David Mazzucchelli**. Everything the stem lists is a decision made in the drawing rather than in the script. Stark shadows and clean lines are matters of ink; deliberate pacing, in a comic, is a matter of how many panels a page is broken into and how they are arranged in tiers, which is again the artist's decision. Auster wrote the original text and Karasik adapted it, so neither is responsible for the look of the finished page.

The three qualities named in that stem — **stark shadows**, **clean lines**, **deliberate pacing** — are worth memorising as a ready description of the book's visual style, because they are the vocabulary a free-response answer needs when it claims the artwork is doing thematic work.

## Keywords

| **Border** | The line or frame around a comic panel |
| **Gutter** | The space between comic panels where the reader infers movement or time passing |
| **Speech Bubble** | A rounded shape that contains a character's spoken words |
| **Emanata** | Visual symbols (e.g., sweat drops, motion lines) showing emotion or movement |
| **Tier** | A horizontal row of comic panels |

# 2 Lexis Terms: The Vocabulary of Postmodernism

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The second half of the lexis list

The guide's lexis list runs on from the comics terms into a second cluster of terms, and this one is about the literary movement the book belongs to rather than the medium it is drawn in. Both clusters are examinable and both are given under the same heading, but they answer different questions: the comics terms describe *how the page works*, and the terms below describe *what kind of book this is*.

## The terms

**Postmodernism** — a literary movement marked by skepticism, irony, and rejection of universal truths or grand narratives. Each of the three markers has a visible consequence in *City of Glass*. Scepticism produces a narrative that will not confirm whether the case was ever real. Irony produces a detective story whose detective is destroyed by detecting. The rejection of grand narratives produces an ending that refuses to resolve, because a resolution would be exactly the kind of universal, tidying truth the movement distrusts.

**Fragmentation** — a narrative technique breaking structure, time, or character continuity into disjointed parts. The definition names three things that can be fragmented, and the book fragments all three: structure (panels and pages break down), time (the surveillance stretches and skips), and character continuity (Quinn is Quinn, then "Paul Auster", then neither).

**Meaning** — often questioned or destabilized in postmodern texts, suggesting multiple or no fixed interpretations. This entry is unusual in that the guide defines not a technique but a thing done *to* meaning. It is the reason the ambiguous ending is not a flaw in the book to be explained away: instability of meaning is the position the text holds, not a failure to reach one.

**Irony** — the use of language or structure to express something opposite or contradictory to the expected meaning. The guide's definition includes *structure*, not just language, which is what licenses a reading of the whole detective plot as ironic: the structure of the genre promises solution, and the book uses that structure to deliver dissolution.

**Intertextuality** — referencing or integrating other texts within a text to create new layers of meaning. The clearest case in the book is the presence of Paul Auster the writer inside a story written by Paul Auster, but the technique also covers the pseudonym "William Wilson" and the Tower of Babel material that Stillman Sr. is obsessed with.

**Genre** — a category or type of literature; postmodernism often blends or disrupts genres. Note the guide's own genre label for this work: *Postmodern Mystery / Existential Graphic Novel / Literary Adaptation*. Three labels rather than one is itself the point.

**Subversion** — undermining traditional norms, values, or expectations, often with a critical or satirical edge. Subversion requires the thing it subverts to be present first; a book cannot undermine detective conventions it never uses. This is why the book takes the trouble to set up a wrong-number case, a troubled investigator, a client and a suspect before dismantling them.

**Text/Paratext** — the main body of a work (text) and supplementary materials like titles, forewords, or footnotes (paratext) that shape interpretation. The distinction matters in an adaptation, where the credits, the framing and the apparatus around the drawn story are themselves interpretive decisions made by the adaptors.

## How the terms connect

The terms are not a random glossary; they describe one coherent programme. **Postmodernism** is the movement, and **fragmentation**, **irony**, **intertextuality** and **subversion** are the techniques by which it acts on **genre** and on **meaning**, while the **text/paratext** distinction marks where the work's boundaries are drawn. When a question asks how the novel functions as a postmodern text, the strongest answers name a technique from this list and then show the effect it has on meaning, rather than asserting that the book is postmodern because it is confusing.

## Keywords

|---|---|
| **Postmodernism** | A literary movement marked by skepticism, irony, and rejection of universal truths or grand narratives |
| **Fragmentation** | A narrative technique breaking structure, time, or character continuity into disjointed parts |
| **Meaning** | Often questioned or destabilized in postmodern texts, suggesting multiple or no fixed interpretations |
| **Irony** | The use of language or structure to express something opposite or contradictory to the expected meaning |
| **Intertextuality** | Referencing or integrating other texts within a text to create new layers of meaning |
| **Genre** | A category or type of literature; postmodernism often blends or disrupts genres |
| **Subversion** | Undermining traditional norms, values, or expectations, often with a critical or satirical edge |
| **Text/Paratext** | The main body of a work (text) and supplementary materials like titles, forewords, or footnotes (paratext) that shape interpretation |

# 3 Core Information, Plot and Premise

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The core information

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Original Author** | Paul Auster (from *The New York Trilogy*) |
| **Adaptors** | Paul Karasik (Writer/Adapter), David Mazzucchelli (Artist) |
| **Genre** | Postmodern Mystery / Existential Graphic Novel / Literary Adaptation |
| **Key Themes** | Identity, Language, Reality vs. Illusion, Authorship, Obsession, Urban Alienation, Failure |

Two things in that table shape everything else. First, the work has **three authors of different kinds** — Auster who wrote the prose, Karasik who adapted it, Mazzucchelli who drew it — in a book whose subject is authorship. Second, the genre line refuses to settle on one label, which is consistent with a postmodern text that blends and disrupts genres rather than obeying one.

The list of key themes is the guide's own shortlist and is worth holding in mind as a checklist while reading the plot: every beat below advances at least one of them.

## Plot and premise

The guide gives the story as a sequence of eight beats.

**Daniel Quinn, a lonely mystery writer grieving his wife and son, receives a wrong-number call meant for "Paul Auster, Private Investigator."** The premise is an accident. Quinn is not sought out, chosen or hired; a telephone rings for someone else. That the whole plot rests on a misdial is the first sign that this is not a story in which events are caused by the detective's competence.

**Intrigued or desperate, Quinn becomes "Paul Auster" and takes the case from the disturbed Peter Stillman Jr.** The guide offers two motives — intrigue and desperation — without choosing between them, and the second is the more useful one for an essay, because it connects the decision to the grief established in the first beat. A man who has lost his family accepts a stranger's identity because his own has become unbearable.

**The case: protect Peter Stillman Jr. from his recently released father, Peter Stillman Sr., who subjected Peter Jr. to horrific language-deprivation experiments.** The commission is protective rather than investigative. Quinn is not asked to find out anything; he is asked to prevent something. This matters later, because a task with no fact to discover cannot be solved, only endlessly performed.

**Quinn begins obsessively trailing the enigmatic and seemingly harmless Stillman Sr. through NYC.** Surveillance replaces detection. The guide's adjectives are careful: *enigmatic* and *seemingly harmless* at once, so that nothing Quinn observes can settle whether there is a threat.

**The investigation spirals into a labyrinth of identities, coincidences, and philosophical questions.** The three nouns are the three ways the case degrades — who people are, what connects to what, and what any of it means.

**Quinn encounters the real Paul Auster (a writer), further blurring lines.** The identity Quinn borrowed turns out to belong to a living person who is not a detective at all.

**Quinn's sense of self and reality disintegrates as the "case" becomes increasingly abstract and unsolvable.** The guide puts *case* in quotation marks at this point, having used the word plainly earlier — by this stage it is no longer clear that there is a case.

**An ambiguous, unresolved ending leaves Quinn lost and broken.** The ending is not withheld information that a careful reader could reconstruct; the guide's word is *unresolved*.

## The premise in the exam

> **1.** What initially prompts Daniel Quinn to take on the role of a detective? a) A newspaper advertisement b) A letter from Peter Stillman Jr. c) A misdirected phone call for "Paul Auster, Private Investigator" d) A request from the real Paul Auster

The answer is **c) A misdirected phone call for "Paul Auster, Private Investigator"**. The three wrong options are each the way a *conventional* detective story might begin — a public advertisement, a written commission from the client, a referral from a colleague — and all three would give Quinn a legitimate route into the case. The correct answer is the only one in which he has no right to be there at all. Note also that the real Paul Auster does not request anything of Quinn; when Quinn eventually contacts him, Auster is indifferent to his plight, so option d) contradicts the character as the guide gives him.

## The ending in the exam

> **4.** How does the graphic novel primarily end for Daniel Quinn? a) He solves the case and returns to writing. b) He confronts and defeats Stillman Sr. c) He finds peace living with Peter Stillman Jr. d) He becomes homeless, mentally broken, and obsessed with indecipherable notebooks, disappearing into the city.

The answer is **d)**. Every element of it is confirmed by the guide: the ambiguous, unresolved ending leaves Quinn lost and broken, his notebooks devolve into gibberish, and the city that has been a labyrinth throughout finally absorbs him. Options a) and b) both supply the resolution the book withholds — one by solving, one by defeating — and c) supplies a consolation the book equally withholds. Recognising that all three wrong answers are forms of closure is the fastest route to the right one.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| ***The New York Trilogy*** | The Paul Auster work from which the story of *City of Glass* is taken |
| **Adaptors** | Paul Karasik (Writer/Adapter) and David Mazzucchelli (Artist), who made the graphic-novel version of Auster's text |
| **Language-deprivation experiments** | The horrific experiments Peter Stillman Sr. carried out on his son, isolating him from language |

# 4 Key Characters

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Daniel Quinn

The **protagonist**: a writer of detective novels under the pseudonym **"William Wilson."** He is emotionally isolated, and he becomes consumed by the case and by his adopted identity.

The essential fact is that Quinn is already living under a borrowed name before the plot starts. Taking on "Paul Auster" is not a new kind of behaviour for him but an escalation of an old one, which is why the borrowed identity takes hold so completely. A man who has been publishing as somebody else has already accepted that the self is something one can put on.

## Peter Stillman Jr.

The **"client."** He is traumatised, and speaks in a unique, broken language as a result of his father's abuse. The guide's summary of his function is that he **represents the failure of language and connection**.

The guide places his quotation marks around *client* for a reason: he supplies a commission but not the ordinary things a client supplies — reliable information, a coherent account of the danger, a means of judging success. He is the theme of linguistic failure standing in the room and speaking.

> **7.** Peter Stillman Jr.'s unique manner of speaking is a direct result of: a) A childhood illness b) His father's linguistic isolation experiment c) A deliberate choice to reject society d) A head injury sustained later in life

The answer is **b) His father's linguistic isolation experiment**. The three wrong options are all *accidents or choices* — illness, injury, personal decision — while the correct one is a deliberate act performed on him by another person. That distinction is the point: Peter Jr.'s damaged speech is evidence of a crime, and it is what makes his father's theories about language something more than eccentricity.

## Peter Stillman Sr.

The **"villain"?** — the guide's question mark is part of the entry and should not be tidied away. He is a former linguist and theologian who conducted cruel experiments on his son, is obsessed with the Tower of Babel and the Fall of Language, and **appears frail and harmless, but his past is monstrous**.

The question mark records a genuine difficulty in the book. A detective story needs a villain for the detective to detect, and Stillman Sr. supplies the biography of one; but nothing he does under Quinn's surveillance is threatening, so the villainy stays in the past tense and never becomes something a detective can act on.

> **2.** Peter Stillman Sr.'s horrific experiments on his son were primarily focused on: a) Physical strength and endurance b) Developing psychic abilities c) Proving a theory about language and the pre-Babel state d) Creating a perfect heir to his fortune

The answer is **c) Proving a theory about language and the pre-Babel state**. It follows directly from what the guide says the man was — a linguist and theologian obsessed with the Tower of Babel and the Fall of Language. Babel is the story of a single original language broken into many; a **pre-Babel state** is the condition of language before that fall, and a father who wished to prove something about it would do so by depriving a child of the languages that came after. The cruelty and the theory are the same act.

## Paul Auster (Real)

A writer Quinn contacts. He **represents the "real" author, indifferent to Quinn's plight**, and he **highlights the theme of authorship and identity**.

The guide's word *indifferent* is the sharp one. The meeting is a disappointment rather than a revelation: the author who might explain Quinn's situation has no interest in it. The separation between an author and the person living inside the story is exactly what the encounter demonstrates.

> **5.** The character of the real Paul Auster in the story primarily serves to: a) Provide Quinn with crucial detective assistance b) Act as a romantic rival for Virginia Stillman c) Blur the lines of identity and highlight themes of authorship d) Offer a scientific explanation for Stillman Sr.'s theories

The answer is **c) Blur the lines of identity and highlight themes of authorship**. Option a) is excluded by his indifference — he assists with nothing — and by the fact that he is a writer, not an investigator. Options b) and d) attribute to him roles the guide never gives him. His function is structural rather than practical: he is the real owner of the name Quinn is using, and his existence is what makes the borrowed identity collapse.

## Virginia Stillman

Peter Jr.'s wife. She is **primarily a conduit for the initial contact and payment**, and she **represents the "normal" world Quinn leaves behind**.

Her small part is a deliberate proportion. She handles the ordinary business of the case — arranging, paying — and once Quinn is inside the surveillance, that ordinary world plays almost no further part in the book.

## The descent, as an essay

The first free-response question asks for Quinn's whole arc:

> **1.** Trace Daniel Quinn's psychological and physical descent throughout the graphic novel. What key events and realizations contribute to his ultimate breakdown and disappearance?

The answer key breaks the descent into seven stages, and reproducing that shape is the surest way to structure the essay, because each stage is a distinct step downward rather than a repetition of the last.

| Stage | Answer key points |
|---|---|
| **Start** | Grieving, isolated writer living through pseudonym (William Wilson) |
| **Catalyst** | Taking on "Paul Auster" identity (initial thrill/replacement) |
| **Obsession** | Stalking Stillman Sr. replaces writing/life; meticulous note-taking (red notebook) |
| **Reality Blurring** | Meeting real Paul Auster undermines his assumed identity; Stillman Sr.'s bizarre behavior defies logic |
| **Loss of Control** | Notebook becomes chaotic/unintelligible; surveillance becomes meaningless/compulsive |
| **Physical Deterioration** | Neglects hygiene, home, health; lives on streets |
| **Breakdown** | Inability to distinguish self/role; language fails; retreats into silence/oblivion; disappears |

Read down the table and the logic of the fall is visible. Quinn begins already living at one remove from himself, adds a second borrowed identity, then replaces his life with the surveillance that identity requires; the two things that could restore him — the real Auster, and the observable behaviour of the suspect — instead remove the ground from under the assumed identity and from under logic itself; his one instrument of order, the notebook, degrades; the neglect of the body follows the neglect of the self; and the end point is the loss of the distinction between the man and the role.

The key also carries an instruction about evidence, which is the marking point most easily missed:

> (Look for specific visual cues: art style changes, panel fragmentation, Quinn's appearance).

The essay is not asking for a plot summary of the descent. It wants the descent evidenced from the artwork — a change in the style of drawing, panels breaking apart, the visible deterioration of Quinn's face and clothing — so an answer that traces the seven stages without pointing at a single page is only half an answer.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Daniel Quinn** | The protagonist; writer of detective novels under the pseudonym "William Wilson", emotionally isolated, who becomes consumed by the case and his adopted identity |
| **Peter Stillman Jr.** | The "client"; traumatised, speaks in a unique, broken language due to his father's abuse, and represents the failure of language and connection |
| **Peter Stillman Sr.** | The "villain"?; a former linguist/theologian who conducted cruel experiments on his son, obsessed with the Tower of Babel and the Fall of Language, who appears frail and harmless but whose past is monstrous |
| **Paul Auster (Real)** | A writer Quinn contacts; represents the "real" author, indifferent to Quinn's plight, and highlights the theme of authorship and identity |
| **Virginia Stillman** | Peter Jr.'s wife; primarily a conduit for the initial contact and payment, and represents the "normal" world Quinn leaves behind |
| **Pseudonym** | The assumed name a writer publishes under — Quinn writes his detective novels as "William Wilson" |
| **Pre-Babel state** | The condition of language before the Tower of Babel, which Stillman Sr.'s experiments on his son were focused on proving a theory about |

# 5 Major Themes

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide lists seven major themes. Five are treated here; the two that the exam turns into full essay questions — the failure of detection and authorship — are taken separately in lesson 6.

## Identity and doubles

Quinn becomes "Auster," and writes as "Wilson." Stillman Sr. and Jr. are **dark reflections** of one another. The real Auster appears. The guide sums the theme up as a **constant questioning: "Who is who?"**

The doubling is systematic rather than incidental. Quinn has two borrowed names, one professional and one adopted in the street; the two Stillmans share a name and stand in the relation of maker to ruined thing; and the name "Paul Auster" belongs at once to a private investigator who does not exist, to a writer inside the book, and to the writer of the book. No character in this arrangement is securely one person, which is why the question the theme generates is not *who did it* but *who is who*.

## Language and meaning

The theme is built from four pieces the guide names together: **Stillman Sr.'s linguistic theories**, **Peter Jr.'s broken speech**, **Quinn's notebooks devolving into gibberish**, and, as the conclusion drawn from them, **the instability and inadequacy of words**.

Set the three cases side by side and they form an argument. Stillman Sr. theorises about a perfect language and produces a son who can barely speak; Peter Jr. is the theory's result; Quinn's notebook is the same failure repeated in a third register, where a man tries to hold a life together in writing and ends with gibberish. Language is attempted as theory, as speech and as record, and fails in each.

## Reality versus illusion and construction

The guide poses this theme as two questions and two observations. **Is the case real? Is Quinn's perception reliable?** **NYC becomes a maze of signs and symbols.** **The graphic novel form emphasises constructed realities.**

The last of those is the most demanding and the most rewarding in an essay. The claim is not merely that the story is about constructed reality but that the *medium* is, because a comic is visibly assembled — drawn frames, chosen viewpoints, gaps between panels that the reader has to fill. A reader of this book is always aware of being shown a made thing, which is a very effective way of unsettling a reader's confidence in what is real.

## Obsession and descent

**Quinn's surveillance becomes all-consuming, leading to his physical and mental unravelling. The case replaces his life.**

Note the direction of causation the guide gives: the physical unravelling is produced by the obsession, not merely accompanied by it. Surveillance is a task with no natural end — nothing is ever discovered, so there is never a reason to stop — and a task with no end will take all the time there is. What makes it a *replacement* rather than an addition is that Quinn gives up writing, home and health to do it.

## Isolation and alienation

**Quinn is profoundly alone. His connections — phone calls, surveillance — are impersonal and ultimately meaningless.**

The guide's examples are the sharp part. Both of the things that link Quinn to other people are forms of contact without presence: a voice on a telephone line, and a man watched from across a street. He is connected to the case constantly and to no person at all, which is why the alienation deepens rather than eases as he becomes busier.

## The artwork as evidence: the second free-response question

> **2.** Analyze how David Mazzucchelli's artwork contributes significantly to the themes of *City of Glass*. Choose TWO specific themes (e.g., Identity, Reality vs. Illusion, Language/Failure, Alienation) and explain how visual elements (panel layout, shading, symbolism, character design, pacing) enhance them.

The question sets a fixed shape: **two themes**, and for each one, **visual elements** plus **an explanation of what they enhance**. The answer key supplies four themes to choose from and, for each, both halves of the answer — the visual evidence and the effect. A response that lists visual features without stating what they enhance has done half of what the key rewards.

| Theme | Visual elements (answer key) | How it enhances |
|---|---|---|
| **Identity** | Use of mirrors/reflections; similar character designs (Quinn, Austers, Stillmans); fragmented panels during identity crises; isolation within frames; visual doubling motifs | Visually shows the instability and dissolution of self |
| **Reality vs. Illusion** | Stark chiaroscuro (extreme light/dark) creating uncertainty; distorted perspectives; dreamlike sequences; panels showing observation/subjectivity (e.g., binocular POV); surreal symbols (falling figures, Tower of Babel) | Creates a constant sense of unease and visual ambiguity, mirroring Quinn's unreliable perception |
| **Language/Failure** | Visual depiction of Peter Jr.'s unique speech bubbles; Quinn's handwriting degrading in the notebook; chaotic scribbles replacing words; visual metaphors for language (mazes, towers); silent panels/sequences | Shows the breakdown of communication and meaning visually, beyond just the text |
| **Alienation** | Wide shots of tiny figures in vast cityscapes; characters framed alone within panels or surrounded by negative space; empty streets; lack of eye contact between characters; use of shadows obscuring faces | Visually conveys profound loneliness, disconnection, and the isolating nature of the urban environment |

Two features of the key are worth noticing when choosing which pair of themes to write on. First, each row draws on a different family of visual technique — **character design** for identity, **shading** and **perspective** for reality, **speech bubbles and lettering** for language, **panel layout and framing** for alienation — so a pair chosen from opposite ends of the table gives an essay more to say than a pair whose evidence overlaps. Second, the evidence named is specific and countable: *mirrors*, *binocular POV*, *negative space*, *shadows obscuring faces*. These are the terms to reach for, rather than general praise of the artwork's atmosphere.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Identity & Doubles** | The theme of constant questioning — "Who is who?" — produced by Quinn becoming "Auster" and writing as "Wilson", by Stillman Sr. and Jr. as dark reflections, and by the appearance of the real Auster |
| **Language & Meaning** | The theme drawn from Stillman Sr.'s linguistic theories, Peter Jr.'s broken speech and Quinn's notebooks devolving into gibberish: the instability and inadequacy of words |
| **Reality vs. Illusion/Construction** | The theme of whether the case is real and whether Quinn's perception is reliable, with NYC as a maze of signs and symbols and the graphic-novel form emphasising constructed realities |
| **Obsession & Descent** | The theme of Quinn's surveillance becoming all-consuming, leading to his physical and mental unravelling as the case replaces his life |
| **Isolation & Alienation** | The theme of Quinn being profoundly alone, his connections — phone calls, surveillance — impersonal and ultimately meaningless |
| **Chiaroscuro** | Extreme light and dark in the artwork, used to create uncertainty |

# 6 The Failure of Detection and the Question of Authorship

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The last two of the guide's major themes are treated together here because the exam treats them as the two full-length essays, and because they are the same argument seen from two sides: a story about a man who cannot solve a case is also a story about a man who cannot author his own life.

## The failure of detection

The guide's entry is four short statements: **it subverts the detective genre**; **the mystery isn't solved — it dissolves**; **the detective fails utterly and is destroyed by the process**.

*Dissolves* rather than *remains unsolved* is the distinction to hold on to. An unsolved mystery is still a mystery: the facts are there and the detective has failed to reach them. A dissolved mystery stops being the kind of thing that has an answer. By the end, it is not clear that there was ever a case, a client's danger, or a crime in progress, so there is nothing for a solution to be a solution to.

The second half of the entry — **destroyed by the process** — is what makes this more than an unhappy ending. In a conventional detective story the investigation is the instrument by which the detective imposes order. Here the investigation is the instrument of his ruin, and the harder he works at it the further he falls.

> **9.** The graphic novel fundamentally subverts the traditional detective genre by: a) Having the detective solve multiple complex cases b) Making the detective a flamboyant superhero c) Depicting the detective's utter failure, mental disintegration, and the unsolvable nature of the mystery d) Setting the story in a fantastical world instead of a city

The answer is **c)**, and it names all three elements of the guide's entry — the utter failure, the disintegration, the mystery that cannot be solved. The wrong options are useful because each is a change to the genre that would *not* be a subversion of it: solving multiple cases fulfils the genre's expectations rather than undermining them, and options b) and d) merely relocate a detective story into a different register or setting. Subversion, as the lexis list defines it, means undermining expectations, so the correct answer must be the one that takes away what the genre promises.

## Writing the genre essay

> **3.** Discuss how *City of Glass* functions as a deconstruction or subversion of the traditional detective genre. What conventional tropes does it use, and how does it ultimately undermine or reject them?

The question is in two parts and the answer key follows the same split, which is the structure to reproduce: first establish the conventions the book *uses*, then show what it does to them. An essay that only argues the book is unconventional has answered the second half of the question with none of the evidence for the first.

**Tropes the book uses**, from the key: the wrong number as case initiation; the troubled detective (Quinn's grief); the mysterious client (Peter Jr.); the potential villain (Stillman Sr.); surveillance; clues (the notebook); and the femme fatale (Virginia — somewhat). The key's own hedge on Virginia is worth keeping, because it is honest about how thin that particular convention is here.

**How it subverts or rejects them**, again from the key, which sorts the subversion into five headings:

| Heading | Answer key points |
|---|---|
| **The Mystery** | Has no clear solution; the "threat" (Stillman Sr.) is ambiguous; clues lead nowhere or become meaningless |
| **The Detective** | Quinn is profoundly incompetent as a detective; his investigation causes his destruction instead of resolution; he lacks the traditional detective's control and insight |
| **Resolution** | No closure; the case isn't "solved" in any traditional sense; justice isn't served; the detective fails utterly and is consumed |
| **Purpose** | Explores philosophical questions (identity, language, reality) rather than delivering a satisfying crime plot |
| **Genre Expectations** | Replaces action and deduction with obsession, paranoia, and psychological collapse |

Read as a set, the five headings dismantle the genre at every level at once — its puzzle, its hero, its ending, its reason for existing, and the pleasures it is expected to provide. That completeness is why the key can call it a deconstruction rather than a variation.

## Authorship and creation

The guide's entry is brief: **Quinn writes fiction and adopts identities; Auster exists as both character and author; the book is a meta-commentary on storytelling and creation.**

The middle claim is the mechanism. Once the same name belongs to a person inside the story and to the person who wrote the story, the boundary between the made and the maker stops being reliable, and the book can raise questions about creation from inside itself rather than by commenting from outside.

## Writing the authorship essay

> **4.** Explore the theme of "authorship" within *City of Glass*. Consider the roles of Daniel Quinn, the real Paul Auster (character), Paul Auster (original author), and Paul Karasik & David Mazzucchelli (adapters). How does the graphic novel comment on the nature of creating stories and identities?

The question names four parties, and the key gives a paragraph's worth of material for each before drawing the commentary together. The four are best understood as four distances from the reader: a character who authors, an author who is a character, an author who is outside the book but appears inside it, and two authors who made the version being read.

| Party | Answer key points |
|---|---|
| **Quinn** | Author of detective fiction under a pseudonym (William Wilson). Creates the "Paul Auster" PI persona. Tries to "author" the reality of the case through his notebook (fails). Becomes a character lost in a narrative he can't control |
| **Real Paul Auster (Character)** | A writer within the story. Represents the "source" of Quinn's assumed identity. Indifferent to Quinn's plight, highlighting the separation between author and character |
| **Paul Auster (Original Author)** | Created the source novel. His presence as a character blurs lines between creator and creation. The story explores themes he wrote about |
| **Karasik & Mazzucchelli (Adapters)** | "Authors" of the graphic novel version. Their choices (visual style, condensation, emphasis) reinterpret Auster's work, demonstrating adaptation as a form of authorship/creation |

The key then states the commentary the essay is meant to arrive at, and these four sentences are the conclusion worth memorising:

- The graphic novel suggests **identities are constructed like stories** (Quinn's personas).
- **Authorship is unstable** (pseudonyms, adaptations).
- **Trying to control a narrative — life or story — can lead to failure and dissolution.**
- **Creation involves layers of identity and interpretation.**

The third of these is where the two essays in this lesson meet. Quinn's investigation and Quinn's notebook are the same attempt made twice: to take a set of events and impose a story on them. The detective fails because the case has no solution, and the author fails because the notebook fills with gibberish, and the book treats both failures as the same failure.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **The Failure of Detection** | The theme by which the book subverts the detective genre: the mystery isn't solved, it dissolves, and the detective fails utterly and is destroyed by the process |
| **Authorship & Creation** | The theme of Quinn writing fiction and adopting identities while Auster exists as both character and author — a meta-commentary on storytelling and creation |
| **Deconstruction** | Taking apart a genre by using its conventional tropes and then undermining or rejecting them |
| **Trope** | A conventional element of a genre — for the detective story, the wrong-number case initiation, the troubled detective, the mysterious client, the potential villain, surveillance, clues and the femme fatale |
