# 7 Motifs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

A motif is a recurring element that accumulates meaning across a work, and in a graphic novel it can recur in the drawing as well as in the words. The guide gives seven, and they are the densest section of the review guide because each one is a piece of ready-made essay evidence.

## The City (NYC) as Labyrinth

NYC is **a character** — vast, anonymous, full of signs and hidden meanings, isolating and disorienting.

Calling the city a character rather than a setting is the claim to argue from. A setting is where events happen; a character acts on the protagonist, and this city does — it swallows Quinn's surveillance, offers him signs that mean nothing, and finally absorbs him entirely.

> **10.** The visual depiction of New York City in the graphic novel primarily emphasizes: a) Its vibrant nightlife and tourist attractions b) Its role as a warm, supportive community c) Its vastness, anonymity, labyrinthine qualities, and function as a character inducing alienation d) Its futuristic technology and architecture

The answer is **c)**, which restates the guide's motif almost word for word and adds the effect: the city *induces* alienation. Note how it is drawn to do so — the answer key for the artwork question names wide shots of tiny figures in vast cityscapes and empty streets, which is vastness and anonymity turned into panel composition.

## The Notebook

The notebook is an archive filled with obsessive and fragmented writings. It begins as Quinn's tool for case notes, then devolves as he loses his grip on reality: the entries shift from surveillance to self-referential doubts, mirroring his disintegration. It also serves as a form of expression.

The trajectory is the meaning. A book that starts as a record of another man's movements ends as a record of the watcher's own doubts, which is a precise measure of how far the case has turned inward.

> **8.** What does Quinn's red notebook symbolize throughout the story? a) His financial success as a writer b) His connection to his deceased son c) His desperate attempt to impose order, meaning, and identity through language – which ultimately fails d) The clues leading to Stillman Sr.'s capture

The answer is **c)**. The three nouns in it — order, meaning, identity — are the three things Quinn loses, and the notebook is where he tries to hold each of them by writing it down. The final clause matters as much as the rest: the attempt *ultimately fails*, which is why the notebook ends in gibberish rather than in evidence. Option d) is the answer a conventional detective story would give, and the book refuses it, since the clues lead nowhere.

## The Telephone

The story begins with the phone call — the start of Quinn attempting to create meaning in his own life. The second phone call is from Auster, who reveals Stillman Sr.'s suicide, and it destroys Quinn's newfound purpose. The guide notes that this marks the end and the start as a callback.

Two calls therefore bracket the entire plot, and they are exact opposites: the first hands Quinn a purpose by mistake, the second removes it by informing him that the man he has been guarding against is dead. Nothing in between was chosen by Quinn, and nothing in between changed the outcome — the telephone gives and takes the case away.

## The Hand and Pen

The pen, first sold to Quinn by a deaf man with the note **"Learn to Speak to Your Friends,"** becomes a symbol of self-expression. As Quinn opens up, his writing grows more subjective — seen in his reflections on homelessness (pp. 102–104), where the handwriting shifts into his own and the narration becomes philosophical. On pp. 88–89, the pen's direction mirrors his emotional state: poised to record Auster's insight, then stunned and inactive when expectations collapse. By pp. 130–131, Quinn is visually submerged, beginning with his pen, symbolising how his identity dissolves with his loss of writing.

The guide draws the conclusion plainly: **his ability to express is his sense of self — once writing fails, so does he.** This is the motif with the most specific page evidence attached, and it is the one to reach for when a question asks how the artwork carries a theme, because all three references are to things visible on the page — the shape of the handwriting, the angle of the pen, the order in which a figure disappears.

The note on the pen is worth reading as a demand the book makes of Quinn and that he never meets. He is told to learn to speak to his friends; instead he uses the pen to record a stranger he watches from a distance, and he has no friends to speak to.

## The Fingerprint

A fingerprint is used to identify people, and in the novel it is used in the form of a maze. It symbolises how Quinn feels lost no matter where he is — his confusion with his identity and with existential meaning.

The image works because it fuses the book's two central problems into one drawing. A fingerprint is the guarantee that a person is uniquely who they are; a maze is the guarantee that a person does not know where they are. Drawing the one as the other says that Quinn's identity *is* the thing he is lost inside.

> **3.** What recurring visual motif is used to symbolize Quinn's psychological breakdown and the labyrinthine nature of reality? a) Floating eyeballs b) Shattered glass c) Mazes, spirals, and fragmented panels d) Flowing water

The answer is **c) Mazes, spirals, and fragmented panels**. The stem asks for two things at once — the breakdown and the labyrinth — and only option c) supplies both: mazes and spirals for the labyrinthine quality, fragmented panels for the psychological collapse. It also links the two motif-level images (the fingerprint maze, the labyrinthine city) to a formal device of the comics page, which is why fragmentation belongs in the same answer as the mazes.

## Eggs

Eggs appear initially along with the Humpty Dumpty analogy. Stillman believes people must be **"broken"** before achieving greater meaning. The guide adds that the motif may also correlate to Quinn's mental fragility, especially after Auster's phone call notifying him about Stillman's death.

The motif carries Stillman Sr.'s theory in a single object: something that must be destroyed to yield what is inside it. Applied to a son, that theory produced the language-deprivation experiments; applied to Quinn, the same image describes a man whose breaking produces no greater meaning at all, which is the guide's quiet judgement on the theory.

## Max Work

Max Work is the protagonist of William Wilson's novels — the detective identity that Quinn envisioned himself being. Quinn has shaped himself through the lens of Max Work.

The chain of names is worth setting out, because questions about identity often turn on it. Quinn writes as **William Wilson**; Wilson's books are about **Max Work**; Quinn models himself on Work; and then Quinn takes the name **Paul Auster** in order to act as a detective. He is imitating a character he invented, under a name belonging to someone else, having published under a name that is not his own either. There is no layer in that stack at which Quinn is simply Quinn.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **The City (NYC) as Labyrinth** | NYC as a character — vast, anonymous, full of signs and hidden meanings, isolating and disorienting |
| **Notebook** | An archive filled with obsessive and fragmented writings; Quinn's tool for case notes, which devolves as he loses his grip on reality, its entries shifting from surveillance to self-referential doubts that mirror his disintegration, and which also serves as a form of expression |
| **Telephone** | The instrument that begins the story with the wrong-number call and ends it with Auster's call revealing Stillman Sr.'s suicide — marking the end and the start as a callback |
| **Hand/Pen** | The pen, first sold to Quinn by a deaf man with the note "Learn to Speak to Your Friends," which becomes a symbol of self-expression: his ability to express is his sense of self, so once writing fails, so does he |
| **Fingerprint** | Used to identify people, and used in the form of a maze in the novel; it symbolises how Quinn feels lost no matter where he is — his confusion with his identity and existential meaning |
| **Eggs** | Appearing with the Humpty Dumpty analogy; Stillman believes people must be "broken" before achieving greater meaning, and the image may also correlate to Quinn's mental fragility |
| **Max Work** | The protagonist of William Wilson's novels; the detective identity Quinn envisioned himself being, and the lens through which he has shaped himself |
